ALREADY FIXED, NOW GUARDED. Closed 2026-11-25.

## The bug was real and is gone

The bead cites pkix-revocation-http/src/cache.rs lines 661 and 846 using SystemTime::now() inside .filter(|e| is_live(e.next_update, SystemTime::now())).

No production code does that any more. Both surviving call sites, now at lines 714 and 941, read:

    let now = SystemTime::UNIX_EPOCH + core::time::Duration::from_secs(self.inner.now_unix);
    ...
    .filter(|e| is_live(e.next_update, now))

So freshness is judged against the caller's now_unix, the same authoritative instant the validator uses. Every remaining SystemTime::now() in the crate is in test code.

Fixed by 0ec06881 "fix(pkix-revocation-http): check anchor-issued certs, cache only verified responses" -- as a side effect of that work rather than as a deliberate close of this bead, which is why the bead stayed open five months after the defect was gone.

The RevocationCache trait documents the avoidance in its own rustdoc: get_crl / get_ocsp return entries WITHOUT freshness filtering, because "this avoids a time-source mismatch between the cache (which would use SystemTime::now()) and the validator (which uses a caller-supplied now_unix epoch timestamp)."

## But nothing stopped it coming back

That was the real gap, and the reason this close has code attached rather than just a note. A P0 sat open for five months while already fixed, and the fix had no regression test. Either half of that is bad; together they mean nobody could tell the difference between fixed and unfixed without reading the source.

Two tests added to cache.rs.

freshness_is_judged_against_now_unix_not_the_wall_clock is the discriminating one. It seeds a cache entry expiring one hour after the pinned NOW of 2026-06-01: in the FUTURE for the validator, months in the PAST by wall clock. A correct cache serves it with no network fetch; a cache reading the wall clock calls it stale and refetches, so the fetch counter becomes 1 and the test fails. The direction is durable because wall clock only ever moves further past a fixed NOW.

a_cache_entry_stale_at_now_unix_is_refetched asserts the converse. It does NOT discriminate on its own -- a wall-clock cache reaches the same verdict -- and is kept so the first test cannot be satisfied by a cache that never expires anything at all.

## Verified the guard fires

Reintroduced the exact bug the bead describes at both call sites. The discriminating test FAILED, the non-discriminating one passed, and both passed again on restore. A guard only ever observed passing has not been tested.

## Why this was P0, stated for the record

A disagreement between the cache's clock and the validator's lands on precisely the deployments that pin time on purpose: offline validation, replaying an archived chain, and any audit expected to reproduce a verdict. Those are the cases where a wall-clock read silently serves data the validator would have rejected, and they are also the cases nobody exercises by accident.

## Acceptance

[x] No production path judges cache freshness by wall clock
[x] Both call sites confirmed to derive their instant from self.inner.now_unix
[x] Regression test added that fails if SystemTime::now() returns
[x] Guard verified by reintroducing the bug rather than assumed
